For unequal dimensions, apply F003 at this v: the larger dimension has infinite measure and the smaller has zero measure, contradicting the inequality in S004 or equality in S005.

R002.fact: For compact K⊆Eucl(n), some L>0 satisfies K⊆[-L,L]^n. Open balls in the specified metric are open, and the positive-integer-radius balls centered at the origin cover Eucl(n).

grounds.reason: E is compact in the specified Euclidean metric.
Each point is a finite tuple with finite Euclidean distance to the origin.

R002.justification: The Archimedean property puts every finite point norm below a positive integer. Balls are open by the triangle inequality. Compactness supplies a finite subcover of these balls; choosing a positive integer at least every selected radius bounds the norm of each point of E. Each absolute coordinate is bounded by the Euclidean norm since its square is a summand in the norm square. This proves the displayed F001 witness existence, also in dimension zero.

R002.fact: For L>0, n≥1 and 0<h≤1, the interval [-L,L] admits a partition into m=ceil(2L/h) closed subintervals of length at most h. Their n-fold products cover [-L,L]^n, number at most (2L/h+1)^n≤(2L+2)^n h^(-n), and have diameter at most sqrt(n)h.

grounds.reason: F001 supplies a positive L whose coordinate box contains E.
The witness L is chosen, n≥1 is the open branch condition, and 0<h≤1 is imposed.
Distances are the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences.

R002.justification: Here m≥1 and m≥2L/h, so equal subdivision gives length 2L/m≤h. Also m≤2L/h+1. Taking Cartesian products gives m^n sets; coordinate differences bounded by h give squared distance at most nh². Multiplying the count inequality by h^n reduces the final estimate to (2L+h)^n≤(2L+2)^n. Thus this verifies the finite grid construction already used in S002.

R002.fact: For finite K>0 and real p>0, Kh^p tends to zero as h decreases to zero, even under any additional fixed positive upper bound on h. Consequently nonnegative H^s_δ(E) bounded above by such admissible-cover costs is zero; if this holds for every δ>0, H^s(E)=0.

grounds.reason: n≥1, s>n, C=(2L+2)^n>0 and the grid gives cost ≤K h^p with K=C n^(s/2), p=s-n>0. The additional bounds are h≤1 and h≤δ/sqrt(n), both positive.
The content is an infimum of nonnegative cover costs, and the measure is the supremum of those contents over positive scales.

R002.justification: For ε>0, choose 0<h<min(1,δ/sqrt(n),(ε/K)^(1/p)). The ordinary monotonicity and inverse identities of positive real powers give Kh^p<ε. Hence each fixed-scale content is at most every positive ε and is zero by nonnegativity. Its supremum over scales is then zero. No limit interchange or measure continuity theorem is required.

R002.fact: For x∈[0,∞] and finite real b≥0, if x≤s for every real s>b then x≤b. This applies with x=D, b=n in S002 and with b=0 in S003.

grounds.reason: D initially lies in the extended nonnegative reals.
N001 is used after the cover estimate to obtain D≤s for each real s>n.
The zero-dimensional branch obtains D≤s for each positive real s and D≥0.

R002.justification: First x≤b+1 excludes infinity. If the resulting finite x were greater than b, the real midpoint s=(b+x)/2 would satisfy b<s<x, contradicting x≤s. For b=0, nonnegativity then yields x=0. The argument does not use real arithmetic on D before proving it finite.

R002.fact: For compact E in a metric space and real δ>0, the balls B(x,δ/4), x∈E, have a finite subcover of E, each with diameter at most δ/2. For any real s>0 this cover has finite total s-cost and is δ-admissible.

grounds.reason: E is compact.
s and δ are arbitrary positive reals and this family is explicitly chosen.
The ambient space carries the Euclidean metric.
Finite covers are admissible countable covers and give upper bounds on H^s_δ(E).

R002.justification: Every center belongs to its positive-radius open ball, so these open balls cover E and compactness gives finitely many. For points y,z in a chosen ball, the triangle inequality gives dist(y,z)<δ/2; taking the diameter supremum gives diam≤δ/2. A nonnegative finite diameter raised to a positive real power is finite, so the finite sum is finite and bounds the infimum defining content. In Eucl(0) every such nonempty ball is a singleton of diameter zero.

R003.fact: For b>0, x↦x^b on nonnegative real numbers is increasing, tends to zero as x↓0, and satisfies (cx)^b=c^b x^b for c,x>0. For a>1, N^{1-a}→0 as positive integers N→∞, and 1/N→0.

grounds.reason: The interval exponent satisfies a>1 and N is a positive integer.
N002 and q>D give q>0, hence q+1>0; the replacement radii are positive.

R003.justification: These are the elementary real-power laws and limits: for x>0 write x^b=exp(b log x). Increasing log and exp give monotonicity and the product law; log x→−∞ at zero gives the first limit. Since N^{1-a}=(1/N)^{a-1}, the integer limit follows. The uses at zero respect 0^b=0 for b>0.

R003.fact: In Eucl(n) with n≥1, a closed ball B(x,rho) of radius rho>0 is nonempty and has diameter 2rho. For any r,eta>0 and q>0 there is such a ball centered at x with 0<diam(B)≤r and diam(B)^q<eta. A nonempty Euclidean set of diameter zero is a singleton.

grounds.reason: The branch assumes n≥1, q>0 has already been derived, and r,epsilon are positive; each zero-diameter covering member is nonempty after empty members are discarded.
The ambient metric is the Euclidean distance on real n-tuples.
Diameter is the supremum of pairwise distances.

R003.justification: The triangle inequality bounds all ball distances by 2rho; the two points x±rho e_1 lie in the ball and attain this value. Choose rho sufficiently small that 2rho≤r and (2rho)^q<eta, using BG001. If diam A=0, all distances between its points vanish, so any chosen point is its only point. This validates precisely the singleton replacements already displayed in S002.

R003.fact: For a nonnegative extended-real infimum h=inf C, if h=0 then for every eta>0 some c∈C satisfies c<eta. Conversely, if for every eta>0 C contains a member of cost below eta, then inf C=0. For the contents defined in D003, H^s(A)=0 implies H^s_delta(A)=0 for each delta>0; if every positive-scale content is zero then H^s(A)=0.

grounds.reason: Each content is an infimum of nonnegative countable-cover costs; the measure is their supremum over positive scales.
N001 gives H^q(E)=0, so S002 uses zero scale content with eta=epsilon/2.
At every fixed scale the displayed interval covers eventually become admissible and have costs tending to zero.
F004 supplies admissible covers at fixed delta with costs below C e0, for every e0>0, where C=2(sqrt(2))^(q+1) is positive and finite.

R003.justification: If no c<eta existed, eta would be a positive lower bound, contradicting inf C=0. Conversely any positive proposed infimum is contradicted by choosing a smaller positive tolerance. Nonnegativity then gives equality to zero. Every scale content is bounded above by their supremum. Supremum of a family of zeros is zero. In S005 choose e0=eta/C, so no exchange of limits or infima is involved.

R003.fact: For 0<t≤1, the integer m=ceil(1/t) is positive and satisfies 1/m≤t and m≤1/t+1≤2/t. A countable union of finite families is countable. If diam U=t and J is an interval of length at most t, then the Euclidean product U×J has diameter at most sqrt(2)t.

grounds.reason: The chosen cover is countable and has 0<r_i≤r≤1.
N_i is defined by the ceiling and each subinterval has length 1/N_i.
Squared product distance is the sum of the squared coordinate distances.

R003.justification: The ceiling lies between 1/t and 1/t+1; reciprocation of positive numbers gives 1/m≤t. Countable pairs (i,j), 0≤j<N_i, form a subset of a countable Cartesian product. Pairwise product distances are bounded by sqrt(t²+t²), hence their supremum is bounded by sqrt(2)t. These facts justify the finite partitions and countability used in S003.

R003.fact: Countable sums of nonnegative extended-real terms admit termwise comparison and regrouping over countable partitions. Also sum_{i≥0}2^{−i−2}=1/2. Consequently the singleton replacements in S002 cost at most epsilon/2, and the grouping of product-cover costs in S004 is valid before finiteness is established.

grounds.reason: Each replacement has q-cost below epsilon 2^{−i−2}; all costs are nonnegative and the original cover costs less than epsilon/2.
W is indexed by the countable original family with finite fibers of size N_i.
Each fiber cost is bounded by N_i(sqrt(2)r_i)^{q+1} and sum_i r_i^q<epsilon.

R003.justification: A nonnegative countable sum is the supremum of its finite subsums. Comparing finite subsums proves comparison; finite subsets of a countably partitioned index set give equality with the iterated sums by taking these suprema. The geometric-series partial sums here are (1/2)(1−2^{−m}), tending to 1/2. The strict original epsilon/2 bound plus the non-strict replacement epsilon/2 bound yields total cost strictly below epsilon. The same comparison and regrouping give exactly the displayed S004 estimate.

R003.fact: If d is a finite nonnegative real number and X∈[0,infinity] satisfies X≤d+1+1/j for every positive integer j, then X≤d+1. Likewise X≤a for every real a>1 implies X≤1.

grounds.reason: D is finite and nonnegative.
Discharged F005 gives the bound for every q>D, in particular q=D+1/j.
The n=0 argument gives dimH(F)≤a for every a>1.

R003.justification: A single finite upper bound excludes X=infinity. If the finite X exceeded d+1, choose j with 1/j<X−(d+1) using the Archimedean property, contradicting the assumed bound. For the second claim take a=1+1/j. This checks both final order limits without assuming dimension was already finite.

R003.fact: For delta>0, r_star=min(1,delta/sqrt(2)) lies in (0,1] and sqrt(2)r_star≤delta. The positive finite constant 2(sqrt(2))^(q+1) depends on the fixed q alone.

grounds.reason: delta is arbitrary positive and q remains fixed while e0 decreases to zero.
F004 is universally quantified over r0∈(0,1] and e0>0.

R003.justification: Both entries in the minimum are positive. Its two defining upper bounds give r_star≤1 and r_star≤delta/sqrt(2). Multiplication by sqrt(2)>0 gives the desired mesh. Positivity and finiteness of the constant allow arbitrary cost tolerances at this fixed mesh.

R004.fact: If V is a nonempty subset of Eucl(n)×R with finite diameter rho, both coordinate projections are nonempty and have diameter at most rho. Its last-coordinate image B is bounded and has real infimum and supremum with sup B−inf B≤rho.

grounds.reason: The product distance is sqrt(||x−y||_2^2+|t−u|^2).
L1 and T restrict to nonempty V_i of diameter rho_i≤delta<infinity.

R004.justification: Each coordinate distance is at most the product distance. Taking suprema of pairwise distances proves the diameter bounds. Fixing one point of B bounds every other point within rho. Real completeness supplies its infimum and supremum. From b≤b'+rho for all b,b'∈B, taking first the infimum in b' and then the supremum in b gives sup B≤inf B+rho.

R004.fact: For a nonempty bounded B⊆R of span at most rho and eta>0, J=(inf B−eta/2,sup B+eta/2) is bounded, open and contains B, with lambda(J∩I)≤rho+eta. For T⊆N and eta_i=epsilon 2^(−i−1)/(1+rho_i^s), sum_{i∈T} eta_i rho_i^s≤epsilon.

grounds.reason: F001 gives bounded nonempty B_i, their span bounds and finite nonnegative rho_i.
epsilon>0, s>0 and the exact eta_i formula are supplied.
Lebesgue measure has the specified open-interval length values.

R004.justification: The strict endpoint enlargement contains every point of B even for span zero. Interval length equals span+eta, and measure monotonicity bounds its intersection with I. Each weighted eta_i is at most epsilon 2^(−i−1). The first m geometric weights sum to 1−2^(−m); their supremum is 1, since 2^(−m) tends to zero. Every finite subfamily of T is contained in an initial segment of N, so its geometric sum is at most 1; taking the supremum over finite subfamilies proves the claimed series bound.

R004.fact: For s>0, the map r↦r^s is increasing on nonnegative real numbers, has 0^s=0, and finite input gives finite output. Thus a countable delta-cover with diameters bounded by rho_i has s-cost at most sum rho_i^s. A constant nonnegative coefficient times an indicator of an open subset of R is Borel measurable and hence almost-everywhere measurable for any measure on this Borel space.

grounds.reason: F001 bounds diam(A_i) by finite rho_i≤delta.
F002 gives open J_i.
The slice-cover construction and the finite coefficients rho_i^s are explicit.

R004.justification: For positive arguments use r^s=exp(s log r) and monotonicity of log and exp; the zero endpoint follows from the positive-exponent convention. Apply this termwise to the covering costs. An indicator of a Borel set takes two constant values on measurable pieces, so it and its constant multiple are measurable. Measurability supplies almost-everywhere measurability for the restricted measure as well.

R004.fact: For nu=lambda restricted to I, a nonnegative constant c has integral c because nu(R)=lambda(I)=1. If c≤g on I for measurable nonnegative g, then c≤integral g dnu. For a Borel J and finite a≥0, integral a 1_J dnu=a lambda(J∩I).

grounds.reason: I is the Borel closed interval [0,1].
The integral is nonnegative extended Lebesgue integration and lambda(I)=1.
c and the coefficients rho_i^s are finite and nonnegative.
F003 gives the pointwise inequality on I and measurable summands.
J_i are open, hence Borel.

R004.justification: The nonnegative integral is defined by measurable simple functions below the integrand. This directly makes it monotone and gives the indicator formula; constant functions are the special case J=R. The measure outside I under the restriction is zero, so the pointwise inequality on I is an almost-everywhere inequality. The countable sum is measurable as the increasing limit of its measurable finite partial sums. Thus monotonicity applies before the explicit M001 interchange.

R004.fact: Nonnegative countable series permit termwise comparison and satisfy sum_i(a_i+b_i)=sum_i a_i+sum_i b_i in [0,infinity], without summability assumptions. For finite rho≥0 and s>0, rho^s rho=rho^(s+1), including rho=0.

grounds.reason: rho_i are finite and nonnegative.
The interval measure bounds and weighted error series bound are available.
All series terms are nonnegative and s>0.

R004.justification: A nonnegative countable sum is the supremum of its finite subsums, which gives comparison. Finite distributivity followed by suprema gives addition of the series: finite subsums of two families can be bounded together using the union of their finite index sets. For rho>0 the power identity follows from exp((s+1) log rho)=exp(s log rho)rho; for rho=0 both powers vanish since both exponents are positive.

R004.fact: If finite c≥0 and K∈[0,infinity] satisfy c≤K+e for every real e>0, then c≤K.

grounds.reason: F001 supplies finite c.
F004 supplies the inequality for every positive e0, with K independent of e0.

R004.justification: For K=infinity the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise K is real; if c>K, choose e=(c−K)/2>0, contradicting c≤K+e. No exchange of limits, covers or integrals is involved.

R004.fact: If c∈[0,infinity] is a lower bound for the costs of all admissible covers, then c is at most their infimum, with the infimum of no costs equal to infinity. Deleting empty members or padding with empty sets preserves a positive-exponent countable cover cost.

grounds.reason: D003 defines H as the infimum of countable cover costs with empty members costing zero.
F005 bounds the cost of an arbitrary cover under L1.
L1 is discharged and the positive parameters s,delta are universally closed.

R004.justification: The infimum is the greatest lower bound in the complete ordered set [0,infinity]; hence every lower bound lies below it, also for an empty family. Countable families admit natural-number indexing with empty padding (finite and empty families included); empty contributions are zero and do not change a nonnegative sum.

R005.fact: For families x_delta,y_delta in [0,infinity] indexed by delta>0, if sup_delta x_delta=infinity and x_delta≤y_delta for every delta, then sup_delta y_delta=infinity. If x_eta≥x_delta whenever 0<eta≤delta, then for every finite M there is delta_0>0 such that x_eta>M for all 0<eta≤delta_0.

grounds.reason: The measures in S001–S002 are suprema over positive scales of extended nonnegative contents.
N001 supplies H^s(E)=infinity; the displayed cover restriction proves scale monotonicity.
N004 gives the pointwise comparison for the positive exponent and scale fixed locally.

R005.justification: If every x_delta were at most a finite M, M would bound their supremum. Thus some x_delta_0>M, and monotonicity propagates this to smaller positive scales. The comparison then gives y_delta_0>M for every finite M, forcing its supremum to be infinity. This uses only the defining least-upper-bound property.

R005.fact: For a finite real d>0 and X∈[0,infinity], if X≥s+1 for every real 0<s<d, then the sequence s_j=d(1−1/j), integers j≥2, has 0<s_j<d and s_j↑d, and its bounds imply X≥d+1.

grounds.reason: N002 proves D finite.
L1 supplies D>0.
F002 gives the bound for arbitrary 0<s<D, generalized with L2 discharged in S003.

R005.justification: For j≥2, 0<1−1/j<1; multiplication by d>0 gives the required range. The gaps d−s_j=d/j decrease to zero: for any epsilon>0 the Archimedean property supplies an integer j>max(1,d/epsilon). If X=infinity the conclusion is immediate. If X is finite and X<d+1, choose such j with epsilon=d+1−X. Then s_j+1=d+1−d/j>X, contradicting its bound. This verifies the stated sequence-limit step without changing the route.

R006.fact: For q>0, N^(-q)→0 through positive integers N; also 1/N→0. In S001 q=a-1>0, so the equal-interval covers eventually have diameter at most any fixed delta>0 and a-cost below any fixed eta>0.

grounds.reason: a>1, N is a positive integer, and the displayed mesh and cost are 1/N and N^(1-a).

R006.justification: Real powers on positive numbers are defined by exp(r log x), giving the usual monotonicity and inverse identities. Given delta,eta>0, choose an integer N larger than both 1/delta and eta^(-1/q). The stated bounds follow. Thus every fixed-scale infimum is zero; its supremum over scales is zero.

R006.fact: Every nonempty subset V of R of finite diameter rho is bounded, has real endpoints l=inf V and u=sup V, and u-l=rho. For every h>0 the interval (l-h,u+h) contains V and has length rho+2h. A countable family can be enumerated with empty padding, and its nonempty indices form a countable subset of N.

grounds.reason: Under L1 each nonempty V_i has diameter rho_i≤delta<infinity; epsilon>0 gives h=epsilon 2^(-i-2)>0.
Diameter is the supremum of pairwise distances.
Lebesgue measure of an open interval is its length.

R006.justification: For a fixed v in V, all points lie in [v-rho,v+rho]. Real completeness gives l,u. Every pairwise distance is at most u-l, while points approaching the infimum and supremum have distances approaching u-l; hence the diameter equals u-l. Strict enlargement then gives containment and the displayed length. Countability permits an enumeration, padding finite lists by empty sets; deleting empty members does not alter the union or positive-exponent cost. These are routine facts for the actual intervals constructed in S002.

R006.fact: Measures, including lambda, are monotone and have the function-like outer-measure structure required by M005. For nonnegative countable families, sums preserve inequalities and split over addition; for T⊆N, sum_{i in T}2^(-i-1)≤1. Consequently sum_{i in T}(rho_i+epsilon 2^(-i-1))≤sum_{i in T}rho_i+epsilon. For fixed C in [0,infinity], if 1≤C+epsilon for every real epsilon>0, then C≥1.

grounds.reason: lambda is the standard Lebesgue measure.
T⊆N, rho_i≥0, epsilon>0, and I⊆union J_i.
V,T,rho remain independent of epsilon; M005 supplies the countable union bound.

R006.justification: Countable additivity on disjoint sets yields monotonicity by splitting B as A and B\A, and yields the outer-measure union inequality by disjointification; thus a measure satisfies the structure stipulated by M005. Nonnegative series are suprema of finite partial sums, so comparison and addition follow by finite sums and cofinal finite unions. The geometric partial sums of 2^(-i-1), starting at i=0, are 1-2^(-m), with supremum 1; a subseries is no larger. If C is finite and C<1, choosing epsilon=(1-C)/2 contradicts 1≤C+epsilon; the infinite case already satisfies C≥1.

R006.fact: For fixed finite c>0 and nonnegative terms x_i,y_i, x_i≥c y_i for every i implies sum_i x_i≥c sum_i y_i, with the usual extended nonnegative interpretation. If every admissible cover cost is at least b, its infimum is at least b. If H_delta is unbounded over positive delta, sup_{delta>0}H_delta=infinity.

grounds.reason: c=delta^(s-1) is finite positive; x_i=rho_i^s, y_i=rho_i, and F003 gives sum_i y_i≥1.
H^s_delta is the infimum over cover costs and H^s the supremum over positive scales.

R006.justification: Finite-sum comparison followed by the supremum over finite subsets proves the series inequality; multiplication by a fixed positive finite constant commutes with that supremum, including an infinite value. The infimum statement is the defining greatest-lower-bound property (also valid for an empty family); the supremum statement is its corresponding least-upper-bound property. These justify the existing cover-to-content and content-to-measure steps.

R006.fact: For d in [0,infinity], bounds d≤a for every real a>1 and d≥s for every real 0<s<1 imply d=1.

grounds.reason: N001 and the equal-interval covers give d=dimH(I)≤a for every a>1.
N001 and the divergent lower costs give d≥s for every s in (0,1).

R006.justification: The upper bounds imply d is finite, for example d≤2. If d>1, choose a=(1+d)/2, contradicting d≤a. If 0≤d<1, choose s=(1+d)/2, contradicting d≥s. Hence both d≤1 and d≥1 hold, exactly as S001 and S005 conclude.

R006.fact: For 0<s<1 and 0<x≤d with d>0, x^(s-1)≥d^(s-1), so x^s≥d^(s-1)x. For x=0 both sides of the latter inequality are zero. Also d^(s-1) is unbounded as d>0 decreases to zero.

grounds.reason: s is fixed in (0,1), delta>0, and under L1 every rho_i lies in [0,delta].
The proof separates rho_i=0 from rho_i>0 before dividing by rho_i.

R006.justification: Writing q=1-s>0 gives x^(s-1)=1/x^q. Positive powers are increasing, so reciprocals give the required reversed inequality. Positive-exponent powers at zero are zero. For every M>0, choosing 0<d<M^(-1/q) gives d^(s-1)>M, which justifies the later unbounded-scale conclusion without a limit exchange.

grounds.reason: The distance calculation uses t,u∈I, hence real by D006.
I is the real interval [0,1].
The Euclidean product distance is the nonnegative square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences.

R007.justification: The real number |t-u| is nonnegative and its square is 0+|t-u|^2. By the defining uniqueness of the nonnegative square root, that square root equals |t-u|.
